chapter: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
title: Curtis Moseby as businessman and leader in name only
summary: Moseby, a pitty-pat drummer, never played with his two bands.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: He put it together for that opening?
Well, he got the job, so it ended up it was Curtis Moseby's orchestra. He was a pitty-pat drummer, not really a great drummer. But --
Oh, he was one of the slickest business-

men ever known outside of the Jewish locality. We used to call him a black Jew. He knew how to maneuver and knew business. If he had -- if only he had been a white man, he would have been a multimillionaire because he knew how to maneuver things.
When you worked in his band at the Apex, did he actually play or was (inaudible)? he just, . . . ?
Did he conduct, (inaudible)? was he the leader, was he there?
He didn't do anything. He only carried his name. The band only carried his name.
And the name got spread all around, huh? (inaudible).
The drummer in that band was Baby Louis, a fellow by the name of Baby Louis, that was a very good drummer as well as a very accomplished trumpet player.
Did he have more than one band? I mean, like when you went to San Francisco (inaudible) did he have...?
He had two bands then, because he kept both places open.
Right, both of them were his. The Lester Lanin of the day.
